This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $k\geq 2$ and let $g_k(n)$ be the largest possible size of $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that every $m$ has $<k$ solutions to $m=a_1a_2$ with $a_1<a_2\in A$.
Is it true that\[g_3(n)=\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+(c+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}\]for some constant $c$?
#796: [Er69,p.80]
number theory
Erdős [Er64d] proved that if $2^{r-1}<k\leq 2^r$ then\[g_k(n) \sim \frac{(\log\log n)^{r-1}}{(r-1)!\log n}n\](which is the asymptotic count of those integers $\leq n$ with $r$ distinct prime factors).
In particular the asymptotics of $g_k(n)$ are known; in [Er69b] Erdős discussed the second order terms, and this question is implicit (especially when compared to the explicit question [425] he asked on several occasions). 
In [Er69] this question actually appears with a denominator of $(\log n)^2$ in the second term. Furthermore, for $k=3$ he claims he could prove the existence of some $0<c_1\leq c_2$ such that\[\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_1\frac{n}{(\log n)^2}\leq g_3(n)\leq \frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_2\frac{n}{(\log n)^2}.\]This is strange, since in [Er64d] both the upper and lower bound techniques that he used in fact prove\[\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_1\frac{n}{\log n}\leq g_3(n)\leq \frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_2\frac{n}{\log n}\]for some constants $0<c_1\leq c_2$. My best guess is that the denominator of $(\log n)^2$ in [Er69] is just an unfortunate repeated typo, and $\log n$ was intended in both the reported bounds and the main question.
This correction is thanks to Tang, who noted independently (see the comments) the improved lower bound given above (indeed with an improvement in the constant $c_1$).
The special case $k=2$ is the subject of [425].
Additional thanks to: Rishika Agrawal, Terence Tao, and Quanyu Tang

 I wrote a short note showing that the asymptotic currently stated on this page cannot be correct.
In the note I give an explicit construction proving\[g_3(n)\ge \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n} + (M+1+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n},\]where \(M\) is the Meissel--Mertens constant. In particular, this rules out any conjectural asymptotic of the form \(g_3(n)=\frac{n\log\log n}{\log n} + (c+o(1))\frac{n}{(\log n)^2}.\)
Motivated by this, a natural revised question is whether there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$,\[
g_3(n)\le \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+c\frac{n}{\log n}.
\]Finally, as discussed in Section 3 of the note, Erdős' bound in [Er64d] yields\[
g_3(n)\le \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+O\!\left(\frac{n}{(\log n)^{1+\delta}}\right)
\]for some $\delta>0$.

 Aha, thanks! In fact this construction is very similar to that given by Erdős in [Er64d] when he proved the lower bound of the given asymptotic. That was just taking the set of all products of two primes $p<q$ with\[\frac{n}{\log n}<pq<n\]and\[(\log n)^2 < p < q^{1/4}.\]The number of such pairs Erdős records as\[(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}\]but, as you note, it's a classical fact that in fact it's equal to\[\frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+(M+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}.\]Your construction is basically this (albeit a little simpler, taking advantage of fixing $k=3$), together with the set of all primes as well. But even just taking the product of two primes already gives a second order term $\gg \frac{n}{\log n}$. 
This makes the denominator of $(\log n)^2$ in the problem here strange, since Erdős' construction already disproved it. Perhaps this was a typo in [Er69]? Or maybe he'd miscalculated the asymptotics.
Also, there is something strange in that this two-primes construction lower bound also contradicts the\[g_3(n)\leq \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+O\left(\frac{n}{(\log n)^{1+\delta}}\right)\]upper bound you mention here. So is there also an error in this upper bound?
EDIT: Ah, yes, Erdős' proof actually gives an upper bound of\[g_3(n) \leq \frac{n\log\log n}{\log n}+O\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right),\]so he's wrong on the final page where he says the bound you mention. In Erdős' upper bound proof he early on discards those integers which may themselves be primes (which of course may contribute $\asymp \frac{n}{\log n}$ to the count). I think that his bound of $\frac{n}{(\log n)^{1+\delta}}$ is only for the error term after some initial pruning of $A$ (e.g. discarding elements of $A$ which are prime or a prime multiplied by a small integer). Looking at Erdős' upper bound proof I do wonder if just sharpening this up a bit would already give an asymptotic for the second order term.

 Thanks - the second part having $g_k$ rather than a $g_3$ is definitely just a typo on my part (indeed it's contradicted by the general asymptotic in the remarks!)
I agree that the question as I have written is implicit; I was trying to avoid simply stating Erdős' bounds and then asking 'can this be improved?'. Indeed, to be pedantic, Erdős never explicitly asked this or posed this as a problem; I just liked the result and wanted to include it on the site as a signpost to an area Erdős had thought about that still had some uncertainty (and would argue that he did implicitly pose this, or at least the case $k=3$, as a problem).

The starting point of the result is the Note by Tang (2026).

A full proof 
claimed by Colin Snyder (using GPT 5.6 (custom harness)).
 Summary:
 We claim the answer is yes: the constant $c$ exists, and equals the Mertens constant plus an explicit variational limit. Formally, with $g_3(n)$ the largest size of $A\subseteq{1,\dots,n}$ such that every $m$ has fewer than $3$ representations $m=a_1a_2$ with $a_1<a_2\in A$, the normalized residual
[\frac{g_3(n)-n\log\log n/\log n}{n/\log n}]
converges. Proved in Lean 4 / Mathlib (closed theorem Erdos796.erdos796_statement, hypothesis-free), standard axioms only, no sorry.
Idea: the main term comes from taking primes and near-primes; the second-order term is a trade-off between smooth numbers kept below the threshold and the multiplication-collision budget. The upper bound is closed by two gates (a smooth-remainder gate and an extracted-tail gate) that convert every admissible set's excess into that budget; a matching construction attains the same variational value. Both meet at $c=M+\lim$ of the explicit variational sequence, where $M$ is the Mertens constant.
 Notes:
 The formal statement was pre-registered and audited quantifier-for-quantifier against the problem text ($a_1<a_2$, so $b=c$ squares are excluded, matching the site). The workspace contains incidental native_decide lemmas and the PrimeNumberTheoremAnd fork; the kernel axiom report ([propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], no sorryAx, no ofReduceBool) proves neither enters the final theorem's dependency cone, as documented in the bundle README. Verify: run check_answer/verify.sh (8,737 jobs), then "#print axioms Erdos796.erdos796_statement".
